scope: Nationwide Medicare benefit rules with national public formulary analysis and named plan examples; clinical studies do not independently establish reimbursement.

items.population: People experiencing menopause; much evidence concerns postmenopausal women
items.policy_summary: All analyzed unsuppressed plan segments listed at least one generic oral estradiol product. Blue Medicare Essential Plus lists 0.5/1/2 mg tablets at Tier 1. No nationwide exclusion of generic estradiol was found.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; Blue Medicare Essential Plus HMO-POS, September 1, 2026, printed page 58.
items.comparison: Compare hormone replacement with testosterone for documented hypogonadism; Viagra for erectile dysfunction has a different statutory treatment.
items.disparity_evidence: Broad formulary listing is counterevidence to a blanket female-hormone exclusion; it does not establish affordability, successful claims, or equal treatment.
items.evidence_type: National descriptive formulary analysis; plan policy; observational outcomes
items.limitations: Listing does not cover every manufacturer, diagnosis, or claim. Oral systemic estrogen cannot be treated as clinically equivalent to vaginal estrogen or every testosterone use.
items.next_question: What are age-specific denial rates, patient costs, and exceptions for the same indication?

items.item: Transdermal estradiol patches and topical gels
items.population: People experiencing menopause who need systemic therapy
items.policy_summary: The national snapshot shows wider listing of generic patches than gels. Blue Medicare Essential Plus lists patches at Tier 3 and gel at Tier 4; route and formulation matter.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; selected plan September 1, 2026. See separate national formulary results.
items.comparison: Compare with oral estradiol and testosterone gel while accounting for indication, clinical suitability, and formulary alternatives.
items.disparity_evidence: Route-specific access differences are observed; their cause and clinical consequences are not established by listing data.
items.evidence_type: National descriptive formulary analysis; plan policy; observational outcomes
items.limitations: Formulations are not interchangeable for every patient. Observational route comparisons cannot establish causal superiority or prove discriminatory restrictions.
items.next_question: How often are a clinically preferred route and its exception denied?

items.item: Low-dose vaginal estradiol: cream, insert/tablet, or local ring
items.indication: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause, including vaginal dryness and atrophy-related painful intercourse
items.policy_summary: Generic cream appears in all analyzed unsuppressed plan segments; inserts and Estring vary. Selected Blue Medicare tiers differ by formulation. These atrophy treatments are not categorically excluded merely because symptoms affect sexual activity.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; selected plan September 1, 2026. Local Estring is distinct from systemic estrogen rings.
items.comparison: Compare local formulations and nonhormonal moisturizers; erectile-dysfunction medicines address a different condition and benefit exclusion.
items.disparity_evidence: A Medicare study reports rising spending per treated beneficiary for selected vaginal-estrogen products; national listing contradicts a blanket exclusion. Direct evidence of sex-based denials is absent.
items.evidence_type: Medicare prescribing/cost study; randomized trial; systematic review; formulary analysis
items.limitations: Cost study may be affected by product selection and generic substitution. A 302-person trial found no additional symptom benefit over placebo; broader review finds some benefits with low certainty.
items.next_question: Which formulation provides accessible treatment for patients unable to use covered cream?

items.indication: Menopausal vasomotor symptoms when endometrial protection is needed
items.policy_summary: Blue Medicare Essential Plus lists estradiol/norethindrone combination tablets at Tier 4. Coverage and age-related prior authorization vary by plan and product; there is no universal prohibition on combined menopausal therapy.
items.policy_scope: Selected plan September 1, 2026; not a census of all combination regimens or standalone progesterone.
items.comparison: Compare complete regimens, including progestogen, rather than estrogen alone in patients with a uterus.
items.disparity_evidence: Product and age rules can burden access; historic randomized safety findings provide relevant counterevidence to interpreting every restriction as sex bias.
items.evidence_type: Plan formulary; randomized clinical evidence; Medicare observational outcomes
items.limitations: WHI studied oral conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone for chronic-disease prevention. It cannot determine the benefit-risk balance of every modern formulation, symptom indication, or younger patient.
items.next_question: Are restrictions aligned with formulation-specific evidence and individualized clinical risk?

items.indication: Moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms due to menopause
items.population: People with menopausal vasomotor symptoms, including those avoiding hormones
items.policy_summary: Listing varies nationally; most listing segments flag prior authorization for every listed option. Blue Medicare Essential Plus lists 45 mg at Tier 4 with prior authorization and a quantity limit.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; selected plan September 1, 2026, printed page 47.
items.comparison: Compare with systemic estrogen when suitable and other nonhormonal treatments; differences in price and safety must be examined.
items.disparity_evidence: Coverage friction is measurable; evidence does not show whether restrictions cause unequal access relative to clinically comparable male treatments.
items.evidence_type: National formulary analysis; randomized efficacy trial; FDA safety communication
items.limitations: SKYLIGHT 1 enrolled women aged 40–65. Short trials cannot establish safety in older Medicare populations; FDA subsequently added a serious liver-injury warning and monitoring requirements.
items.next_question: Do prior authorization criteria allow exceptions for contraindications or intolerance to alternatives?

items.policy_summary: The August 2026 basic formulary file lists the menopause-specific 7.5 mg capsule in some formularies. Do not infer its coverage from generic paroxetine antidepressant tablets.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; RxCUI 1430122 independently mapped in the CMS reference file.
items.comparison: Compare approved 7.5 mg capsules with other nonhormonal therapies; alternative paroxetine doses have different labeling and coverage questions.
items.disparity_evidence: Variation within the same active moiety is a concrete access question; neither formulation preference nor clinical efficacy establishes sex discrimination.
items.evidence_type: National formulary record; two randomized efficacy trials
items.limitations: This supplementary screen is separate from the original drug-group table. Off-label alternatives require their own medically accepted indication and benefit assessment.
items.next_question: Do plans offer a usable nonhormonal option when estrogen is inappropriate?

items.indication: Moderate-to-severe dyspareunia or vaginal dryness due to menopausal vulvovaginal atrophy
items.population: Postmenopausal women with symptomatic vulvovaginal atrophy
items.policy_summary: Ospemifene is listed in a minority of analyzed basic formularies; prior authorization is common where listed. Basic listing confirms that atrophy-related painful intercourse is not automatically treated as excluded sexual dysfunction.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; see separate national listing and prior-authorization table.
items.comparison: Compare with vaginal estrogen and prasterone for the same atrophy symptoms, accounting for route and contraindications.
items.disparity_evidence: Access is substantially narrower than generic vaginal estrogen. The data identify a formulation/therapy difference, not its cause or a male-female causal disparity.
items.evidence_type: National formulary analysis; systematic review of randomized trials
items.limitations: Low-certainty short-term efficacy evidence; no proof of superiority for all patients. Nonlisting does not determine exception outcomes or final reimbursement.
items.next_question: Are covered alternatives clinically feasible and exceptions timely for patients who cannot use vaginal products?

items.indication: Moderate-to-severe dyspareunia due to menopausal vulvovaginal atrophy
items.population: Postmenopausal women with atrophy-related painful intercourse
items.policy_summary: Prasterone appears in very few analyzed basic formularies. Its presence demonstrates eligibility for this atrophy indication; a plan-specific exception may still be relevant when it is absent.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; see separate national listing table.
items.comparison: Compare with vaginal estrogen and ospemifene for the same symptom, rather than medicines for desire or erectile dysfunction.
items.disparity_evidence: Very narrow listing suggests a potential access barrier, but unmet need, denials, substitution, cost, and disparate impact were not measured.
items.evidence_type: National formulary analysis; systematic review of randomized trials
items.limitations: Evidence suggests short-term symptom benefit with low certainty. Limited long-term comparative data do not establish that all patients require this product.
items.next_question: Which patients lack an effective covered alternative, and what happens to their exception requests?

items.item: Sildenafil or Viagra for erectile dysfunction
items.policy_summary: Federal statute excludes drugs when used for sexual or erectile dysfunction from the basic Part D benefit. Supplemental coverage may exist. Sildenafil prescribed for an eligible nonsexual indication, such as pulmonary arterial hypertension, is a separate case.
items.policy_scope: Nationwide statutory exclusion; individual supplemental benefits vary. CMS guidance effective for erectile-dysfunction drugs from 2007.
items.comparison: Female HSDD drugs face the same statutory category. Atrophy treatments and pulmonary-hypertension treatment are different clinical uses.
items.disparity_evidence: This is counterevidence to the claim that standard Medicare reimburses Viagra for erectile dysfunction while universally excluding estradiol.
items.evidence_type: Federal statute; CMS benefit guidance; supplemental-plan example
items.limitations: The 2024 national dataset includes 398 Viagra claims, but lacks indication and benefit basis. Those records cannot establish standard Part D erectile-dysfunction coverage.
items.next_question: For a reported paid claim, what were the diagnosis, payer, product, and supplemental benefit?

items.indication: Acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder
items.population: FDA December 2025 label: women younger than 65, including postmenopausal women
items.policy_summary: The statutory exclusion for drugs used for sexual dysfunction applies to HSDD treatment under basic Part D. FDA approval or label expansion does not itself create Medicare reimbursement. A reviewed employer supplemental formulary lists Addyi.
items.policy_scope: Nationwide basic Part D exclusion; supplemental benefits vary. December 2025 FDA label expands beyond premenopausal women.
items.comparison: Compare with sildenafil for erectile dysfunction under the same statutory exclusion, while recognizing different mechanisms and clinical endpoints.
items.disparity_evidence: Women face a coverage gap, but the basic statutory exclusion also reaches male erectile-dysfunction drugs. Unequal supplemental coverage remains an empirical question.
items.evidence_type: Federal statute; FDA label; systematic review and meta-analysis
items.limitations: Meta-analysis found small average benefit and increased adverse events; individual benefit varies. Most age-eligible Medicare beneficiaries are outside the approved age range, while younger disabled beneficiaries may qualify clinically.
items.next_question: Which supplemental plans cover each sexual-health treatment, and with what cost sharing?

items.indication: Acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder
items.population: Premenopausal women meeting the labeled indication
items.policy_summary: Basic Part D excludes drugs used for sexual dysfunction. FDA approval of bremelanotide does not override that exclusion; a supplemental benefit would require separate verification.
items.policy_scope: Nationwide basic Part D statutory rule; current labeling remains limited to premenopausal women.
items.comparison: Compare with flibanserin and erectile-dysfunction drugs; avoid treating all sexual symptoms as the same disease.
items.disparity_evidence: Exclusion affects younger Medicare beneficiaries who meet the indication; the statute is not a female-only exclusion.
items.evidence_type: Federal statute; current drug label; two randomized phase 3 trials
items.limitations: Trial participants were predominantly White, with a mean age of 39. Desire and distress improved; adverse effects and limited older-population evidence matter for interpretation.
items.next_question: Do disabled premenopausal beneficiaries have access through supplemental benefits or other programs?

items.indication: Testosterone deficiency due to an underlying medical condition
items.population: Men with documented hypogonadism; this row does not assess gender-affirming care
items.policy_summary: Testosterone is broadly listed, often with prior authorization. Selected Blue Medicare formulations require prior authorization and some quantity limits. Coverage for replacement must not be conflated with erectile-dysfunction treatment or automatic coverage of age-related low testosterone.
items.policy_scope: CMS August 2026 snapshot; selected plan September 1, 2026, printed page 62.
items.comparison: A useful hormone-replacement comparator for estrogen only after accounting for diagnosis, route, baseline risk, required monitoring, and age.
items.disparity_evidence: Testosterone faces substantial prior-authorization restrictions, providing counterevidence to a claim of uniformly easy access for male hormones.
items.evidence_type: National formulary analysis; plan policy; randomized safety trial
items.limitations: TRAVERSE studied selected men with low testosterone and cardiovascular risk; it does not establish safety or coverage for all ages, indications, or formulations. FDA labeling developments require product-specific review.
items.next_question: How do indication-matched denials, monitoring demands, and patient costs compare with menopausal therapy?

studies.citation: Tabakin AL, Lee W, Winkler HA, Shalom DF. Vaginal Estrogen Prescribing and Cost Trends Among Medicare Part D Beneficiaries. Urogynecology. 2024.
studies.design: Retrospective analysis of Medicare Part D spending and prescriber datasets
studies.population: Medicare beneficiaries receiving the vaginal-estrogen products studied
studies.finding: Reported spending per treated beneficiary rose from $688.52 to $1,027.55, while claims for the products studied decreased. Estrace, Yuvafem, Vagifem, and Estring dominated the reported product distribution.
studies.limitation: Spending is not beneficiary out-of-pocket cost. Product selection and generic substitution may affect trends; observational counts do not establish cost-caused undertreatment or discriminatory denials.
studies.relevance: Direct Medicare cost/utilization evidence; interpret product scope before generalizing to all vaginal estrogen.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Baik SH, Baye F, McDonald CJ. Use of menopausal hormone therapy beyond age 65 years and its effects on women’s health outcomes by types, routes, and doses. Menopause. 2024;31:363–371.
studies.design: Large observational cohort with time-varying adjusted Cox models
studies.population: Approximately 10 million senior women in Medicare records
studies.finding: Estrogen monotherapy after 65 was associated with lower mortality than never use/discontinuation (adjusted HR 0.81). Associations differed by hormone combination, route, and dose.
studies.limitation: Residual confounding, treatment selection, and healthy-user effects prevent causal claims. This is not a randomized initiation trial or a study of coverage denials.
studies.relevance: Direct Medicare outcomes research counters blanket age-based assumptions; interpret alongside randomized evidence and formulation-specific risk.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Mitchell CM et al. Efficacy of Vaginal Estradiol or Vaginal Moisturizer vs Placebo for Treating Postmenopausal Vulvovaginal Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178:681–690.
studies.population: 302 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vulvovaginal symptoms
studies.payer: Clinical trial; not a payer-policy study
studies.finding: Vaginal estradiol 10 mcg tablets and moisturizer did not reduce the most bothersome symptom more than dual placebo over 12 weeks.
studies.limitation: One formulation and short follow-up; substantial placebo improvement. Does not prove all vaginal-estrogen regimens are ineffective or determine treatment for each patient.
studies.relevance: Essential counterevidence; clinical uncertainty must remain visible when interpreting access restrictions.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Danan ER et al. Hormonal Treatments and Vaginal Moisturizers for Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: A Systematic Review. Ann Intern Med. 2024;177:1400–1414.
studies.design: Systematic review of 46 randomized trials; no pooled meta-analysis because of heterogeneity
studies.population: Postmenopausal women with at least one GSM symptom
studies.payer: Mixed trial settings; AHRQ/PCORI-funded review, not Medicare coverage analysis
studies.finding: Vaginal estrogen, vaginal DHEA, and oral ospemifene may improve selected GSM symptoms compared with placebo; certainty was generally low. Moisturizers may improve dryness.
studies.limitation: Most trials lasted 12 weeks or less; inconsistent outcomes and limited long-term safety data. Few enrolled women with prior cancer.
studies.relevance: Supports plausible clinical benefit while preserving uncertainty; does not itself establish coverage or comparative cost-effectiveness.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Lederman S et al. Fezolinetant for treatment of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause (SKYLIGHT 1): a phase 3 randomised controlled study. Lancet. 2023.
studies.design: Phase 3 randomized placebo-controlled trial; 12-week controlled phase and 40-week extension
studies.population: Women aged 40–65 with at least seven moderate-to-severe hot flashes daily
studies.finding: At week 12, fezolinetant 45 mg reduced daily vasomotor-symptom frequency by approximately 2.55 more episodes than placebo and improved severity.
studies.limitation: Participants older than 65 were excluded. Trial efficacy does not resolve real-world affordability or rare liver injury subsequently identified through safety surveillance.
studies.relevance: Evidence for a nonhormonal alternative; coverage rules need separate CMS/plan evidence.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Simon JA et al. Low-dose paroxetine 7.5 mg for menopausal vasomotor symptoms: two randomized controlled trials. Menopause. 2013;20:1027–1035.
studies.design: Two randomized double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials lasting 12 and 24 weeks
studies.population: Postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms; 591 paroxetine and 593 placebo participants
studies.finding: Paroxetine 7.5 mg reduced symptom frequency at weeks 4 and 12. The 24-week study met all four primary endpoints; the shorter study met three of four.
studies.limitation: One severity endpoint was not significant in the shorter trial. Evidence concerns a particular low-dose formulation, not all antidepressant doses or all Medicare patients.
studies.relevance: Establishes a nonhormonal treatment option; cannot establish its formulary status.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Jaspers L et al. Efficacy and Safety of Flibanserin for the Treatment of Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Intern Med. 2016;176:453–462.
studies.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of five published and three unpublished randomized trials
studies.population: 5,914 women with HSDD; eligible studies included premenopausal and postmenopausal women
studies.payer: Mixed trials; no Medicare reimbursement analysis
studies.finding: Flibanserin 100 mg produced about 0.49 additional satisfying sexual events monthly versus placebo. Discontinuation due to adverse effects increased (risk ratio 2.19), alongside dizziness, somnolence, nausea, and fatigue.
studies.limitation: Review graded overall evidence very low; population diversity and comorbidity representation were limited. It predates the December 2025 expanded FDA label.
studies.relevance: Documents both modest average benefit and harms; neither result overrides the statutory Part D exclusion.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Kingsberg SA et al. Bremelanotide for the Treatment of Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder: Two Randomized Phase 3 Trials. Obstet Gynecol. 2019;134:899–908.
studies.design: Two randomized placebo-controlled phase 3 trials; 24-week core phase
studies.population: 1,267 randomized premenopausal women; mean age 39; 85.6% White
studies.finding: Bremelanotide improved measured sexual desire and associated distress versus placebo. Nausea, flushing, and headache occurred more often with active treatment.
studies.limitation: Demographics and indication limit extrapolation to older Medicare women. Changes in desire/distress do not measure reimbursement, affordability, or unequal access.
studies.relevance: Demonstrates a female sexual-health therapy with clinical benefit and tolerability tradeoffs, despite the shared statutory exclusion.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Lincoff AM et al.; TRAVERSE investigators. Cardiovascular Safety of Testosterone-Replacement Therapy. N Engl J Med. 2023;389:107–117.
studies.population: 5,246 men aged 45–80 with hypogonadism and established or elevated cardiovascular risk
studies.payer: Clinical trial; not Medicare coverage analysis
studies.finding: Testosterone gel was noninferior to placebo for major adverse cardiovascular events. Atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury, and pulmonary embolism occurred more often in the testosterone group.
studies.limitation: Selected symptomatic men with repeatedly low testosterone; findings do not establish long-term safety in every population, formulation, or indication.
studies.relevance: Comparator evidence: coverage can coexist with indication limits, monitoring, and meaningful safety concerns.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

studies.citation: Rossouw JE et al.; WHI investigators. Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women’s Health Initiative randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002;288:321–333.
studies.design: Randomized placebo-controlled primary-prevention trial; stopped early after mean 5.2 years
studies.population: 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 with an intact uterus
studies.payer: Federally supported clinical trial; not Medicare policy research
studies.finding: Oral conjugated equine estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone increased important cardiovascular and breast-cancer outcomes while reducing fractures; the overall balance did not favor use for primary chronic-disease prevention.
studies.limitation: A specific oral combination and prevention question; cannot generalize directly to local vaginal estrogen, transdermal estradiol, other progestogens, or every symptom-treatment decision.
studies.relevance: Counterbalances favorable observational findings; historic evidence and updated labeling must be interpreted by regimen and indication.
studies.extraction_level: PubMed citation and abstract; no systematic full-text extraction

supplemental_policy_sources.topic: Part D sexual/erectile dysfunction exclusion; sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension and supplemental coverage
Addyi FDA label, December 2025: women less than 65; not limited to premenopausal women
Veozah FDA warning about rare serious liver injury
2026 FDA menopausal hormone product label revisions; changes are not coverage mandates
Testosterone FDA indication and evolving label information
PSERS 2026 employer supplemental bonus benefit lists Viagra and Addyi; outside national public plan-file scope

formulary_evidence.denominator: 5,499 unsuppressed contract-plan-segment combinations; 5,055 contract-plan pairs; not enrollment weighted.
formulary_evidence.scope_limits: Public file excludes employer plans, PACE, non-Part-D plans, and demonstration plans except MMPs. Listing does not establish every strength, product, indication, payment, or absence of age edits.

supplementary_paroxetine_screen.method: Independent standard-library csv join; basic formulary RxCUI 1430122; unique unsuppressed contract/plan/segment joined by formulary ID. Not added to original national group table.

review_limitations: Targeted literature review, not a prospectively registered systematic review.
Direct Medicare costs/outcomes studies are separated from efficacy trials and statutory coverage rules.
Evidence does not establish causal discrimination by sex, gender identity, or race.
Current label expansions and plan revisions should be checked at the point of care.
All ten scientific study summaries are abstract-based; full articles were not systematically extracted or independently risk-of-bias assessed.
